title: Benford's Law: Why Do Leading Digits Prefer Small Numbers?
question: Why do the first digits of real-world numbers, from river lengths to tax returns, favor 1 over 9?
summary: In many natural datasets about 30% of numbers begin with 1 and under 5% with 9. The pattern comes from scale invariance, and it is now used to catch fraud.
content:
A Strange Regularity

In 1881 the astronomer Simon Newcomb noticed that the early pages of logarithm tables were more worn than the later ones. People were looking up numbers beginning with 1 far more often than numbers beginning with 9. In 1938 the physicist Frank Benford checked this against twenty datasets, including river lengths, street addresses, atomic weights and baseball statistics, and found the same pattern. The probability that the leading digit is d is log10(1 + 1/d). That gives about 30.1% for 1, 17.6% for 2, and 4.6% for 9.

Why Not Uniform?

Intuition says each digit from 1 to 9 should lead equally often. That only holds if numbers are spread evenly on a linear scale, and many quantities are not. Consider something growing 10% a year. Getting from 1,000 to 2,000 takes about seven years. Getting from 8,000 to 9,000 takes about one. The quantity spends far more time with a leading 1 than with a leading 9, simply because each step is a smaller fraction of the current value.

Scale Invariance

A deeper argument comes from asking what a "universal" distribution of first digits would have to look like. If the law is real, it should not depend on units. Prices in dollars and in euros should show the same digit frequencies. Roger Pinkham showed in 1961 that the only distribution of first digits unchanged by rescaling is Benford's. It is uniform on the logarithm of the number, so each order of magnitude is equally likely and, within it, the space between 1 and 2 is much larger than the space between 9 and 10.

When It Works and When It Fails

The law needs data spanning several orders of magnitude and generated by multiplicative processes: growth, compounding, mixing of many sources. Human heights fail because they sit in a narrow band. Telephone numbers fail because they are assigned, not measured. Theodore Hill proved in 1995 that if you draw numbers from randomly chosen distributions and pool them, the leading digits converge to Benford's law, which explains why messy collections like newspaper figures obey it.

Catching Cheats

People inventing numbers tend to spread leading digits evenly, which is exactly wrong. Forensic accountants use this. Mark Nigrini popularized Benford tests for tax returns and ledgers, and the method has been applied to election data, scientific datasets and financial statements. A deviation is not proof of fraud, since many honest datasets are non-Benford, but it is a cheap way to decide where to look.

perspectives.title: The Mathematician
perspectives.description: Benford's law is the unique scale-invariant distribution of leading digits, equivalent to a uniform distribution of the logarithm modulo 1. Many multiplicative processes converge to it.

perspectives.title: The Forensic Accountant
perspectives.description: It is a screening tool. Fabricated figures usually show too few 1s and too many 6s, 7s and 8s, so a digit test can flag a ledger for closer review.

perspectives.title: The Physicist
perspectives.description: A law of nature should not depend on the units we chose, so scale invariance is the natural symmetry. Power-law and exponential growth phenomena then produce Benford statistics automatically.

perspectives.title: The Psychologist
perspectives.description: People are poor generators of randomness and treat 'random' as 'evenly spread'. The law exposes this bias because fabricated data lacks the skew real processes produce.

Scale invariance and renormalization in physics
openQuestions: Is there a single deep reason for Benford behavior in all natural datasets, or only a family of separate mechanisms?
How robust is Benford-based fraud detection against a forger who knows the law?
Why do some physical constants and stock prices follow it closely while others do not?
Can digit tests on elections ever be statistically sound, given legitimate non-Benford structure?
